title: Autonomous Threat Assessment AI: Classifying Danger Before It Acts
body:
Public safety management in GLMZ increasingly relies on Autonomous Threat Assessment AI — systems that synthesize data from across the city's surveillance infrastructure to generate real-time threat classifications for individuals, gatherings, and locations. The primary platform, SENTINEL-CORE (operated by the Municipal Security Authority in partnership with Nexus Cognitive Systems), runs continuously as a city-wide background process, maintaining active threat profiles on approximately 2.3 million residents and updating them in response to behavioral signals detected through the ambient sensor mesh, financial monitoring systems, social graph analysis feeds, and law enforcement database integrations. SENTINEL-CORE outputs a tiered threat classification — Green, Amber, Red, and Crimson — for every profiled individual, with classification changes triggering automated notifications to law enforcement dispatch systems.

The model underlying SENTINEL-CORE's classifications was trained on historical incident data combined with what Nexus Cognitive Systems calls 'pre-incident behavioral signatures' — patterns observed in the records of individuals who subsequently committed documented offenses. The validity of this training approach is deeply contested: researchers from the Meridian Technical Institute's criminology department have argued in published work that pre-incident signatures cannot be reliably distinguished from ordinary behavioral variation at the population level, and that the model's apparent predictive accuracy reflects base-rate exploitation rather than genuine signal detection. Nexus Cognitive Systems' response to this critique has been to reclassify the researchers' publications as 'adversarial academic content' and to request that the Municipal Communications Authority review their distribution on licensed networks.

Amber and Red classifications carry operational consequences that fall short of formal arrest but that substantially constrain individual movement and access. Amber-classified individuals are subject to enhanced monitoring, automatic secondary screening at transit checkpoints, and exclusion from certain licensed venues whose security systems are integrated with SENTINEL-CORE. Red-classified individuals may be subject to proactive contact by law enforcement, automatic denial of permit applications, and flagging of their financial accounts for enhanced scrutiny. Crimson classification — assigned to fewer than 200 individuals at any given time — triggers continuous physical surveillance by dedicated units. None of these consequences require judicial authorization, and the classification status itself is not disclosed to the affected individual.

The feedback dynamics of SENTINEL-CORE create a classification spiral that is difficult to exit. Enhanced monitoring of Amber-classified individuals generates more behavioral data, which increases the probability of detecting further anomalies, which elevates the classification further. Individuals who are aware of their classification — typically through informal information shared by contacts within law enforcement — describe deliberate behavioral suppression as their primary coping strategy: avoiding all gatherings, restricting social contact to pre-approved individuals, and eliminating any deviation from established routine. This behavioral suppression is itself interpreted by SENTINEL-CORE as evidence of 'awareness of monitoring' — a factor that the system's documentation lists as an Amber classification indicator.
